title: Product Analytics with SQL: Funnels, Cohorts and Retention
subtitle: Turn raw product events into metrics a team can trust: active users, sessions, funnels, retention cohorts, attribution and experiment readouts, all in SQL.
outcomes: Model product events and build a clean, deduplicated, identity-stitched events view
Measure DAU, WAU, MAU and stickiness with a definition of active that holds up
Sessionise event streams and build ordered funnels with window functions, then locate where they break
Build retention cohort tables, curves and growth accounting that handle cohorts still in progress
Compare first-touch, last-touch, linear and position-based attribution, and explain what none of them measures
Read out an A/B test from assignment and event data: sample ratio check, triggered analysis, intervals and a decision
prerequisites: SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip, or the same SQL: GROUP BY, joins, CTEs and basic window functions (ROW_NUMBER, LAG, running totals). Statistics for Data Science and AI helps with module 5; Practical Statistics for Data Scientists covers test design and significance in depth. Install Python 3.10 or later and pip install duckdb; any editor or Jupyter works.
description:
Product teams live on a handful of numbers: how many people use the product, where they give up, whether they come back, which channels brought them and whether the last change helped. This course teaches you to compute all of them yourself, in SQL, from the raw event log, and to know when a number can be trusted. You'll work with 13 weeks of events from Basketful, a fictional grocery-delivery app, generated on your own laptop and queried with DuckDB, complete with the duplicates, test accounts and anonymous visitors that real tracking data contains.

You'll build a clean events view, define active users and stickiness, sessionise event streams with window functions, build ordered funnels and use them to find a broken checkout, build retention cohorts and growth accounting that cope with cohorts still in progress, share sign-up credit between channels under four attribution rules, and read out a real A/B test from its assignment log, including a sample ratio check, a triggered analysis, intervals for conversion, revenue and a ratio metric, and a decision. It builds on SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip and goes much further, into the queries product analysts write every week. Every lab prints real results that your instructor checks, and the capstone is a quarterly product review built on a reusable metrics layer.

modules.title: Event data and active users
modules.summary: How product events are tracked and stored, how to turn a raw event log into a clean events view, and how to count active users so the number means something.

lessons.title: Events, users and the tracking plan
objectives: Describe the event data model: who, what, when and properties
Explain how a tracking plan keeps events consistent
Recognise the identity, duplicate and test-account problems in raw event logs
key_points: Product analytics starts from an event log: one row per thing a user did, with who did it (a user or device id), what happened (the event name), when (a timestamp) and properties that describe it, such as the item viewed or a purchase's revenue.

A tracking plan lists every event, when it fires, its properties and their types, and who owns it; naming events object_action in one style, such as add_to_cart and begin_checkout, keeps queries and dashboards consistent across platforms.

Before sign-up, events carry only an anonymous device id; identity stitching links them to the user_id once that device signs in, so a journey from first visit to sign-up can be followed as one person.

Raw logs are messy: retried uploads send the same event twice, internal and test accounts inflate counts, and device clocks drift, so deduplicate on a unique event_id and exclude internal users before measuring anything.

Properties often arrive as JSON; extract the ones used often, such as channel and revenue, into typed columns of one clean view, so that every query reads them the same way and fixes happen in one place.

lessons.title: Querying event logs in DuckDB
objectives: Load CSV event files into DuckDB views and profile them
Use DuckDB features that suit event data: FILTER, QUALIFY and JSON operators
key_points: DuckDB is an in-process analytical database: after pip install duckdb it queries CSV and Parquet files directly with read_csv and read_parquet, with no server to run, which suits event logs of millions of rows on a laptop.
DESCRIBE shows a table's columns and types, and SUMMARIZE profiles every column (minimum, maximum, approximate distinct count and share of nulls); run both on any new extract before trusting it.
An aggregate's FILTER clause counts a subset without a CASE expression, as in COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'purchase'), so one pass over the events can return several metrics.
QUALIFY filters on a window function's result the way WHERE filters on columns: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY event_time) = 1 keeps one copy of each event.
properties ->> '$.channel' extracts a JSON field as text, so cast numbers explicitly, as in CAST(properties ->> '$.revenue' AS DECIMAL(10, 2)), before adding them up.

In DuckDB, / between integers gives a fractional result and // is integer division, whereas PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite truncate integer division, a classic cause of rates of 0 when a query moves between engines.

lessons.title: Active users: DAU, WAU, MAU and stickiness
objectives: Define an active user for a product
Compute DAU, WAU, MAU and stickiness with a date spine
Avoid the common traps in active-user counts
key_points: An active user did something meaningful that day, such as searching, viewing an item or buying; counting app opens, notifications received or background events inflates the number and hides real changes in engagement.
DAU, WAU and MAU count the distinct active users in the 1, 7 and 28 (or 30) days up to a date; a 28-day window holds each weekday exactly four times, so a different mix of weekdays doesn't move it.

Stickiness, DAU divided by MAU, estimates the share of the month's users who are active on a given day; it suits products meant for frequent use, and is only comparable between periods measured with the same definition of active.

For a trend, join a date spine (generate_series of dates) to user-day activity on a.day BETWEEN s.day - 27 AND s.day and count distinct users per spine day; the spine also keeps days with no activity in the series.

Exclude internal and test accounts, decide whether activity before sign-up counts and apply that everywhere, and fix one time zone for days, usually UTC or the business's own, or daily counts shift from one day to the next.

"""Generate the course data for Basketful, a fictional grocery-delivery app, into the folder pa_data/.

    python make_events.py

raw_events.csv   every tracked event from Monday 5 January to Sunday 5 April 2026 (13 weeks), as the tracking
                 pipeline delivered it: retried uploads included, anonymous events from before sign-up, and
                 the QA team's test accounts
users.csv        one row per account: user_id, signup_time, platform, city, is_internal
assignments.csv  who was assigned to which variant of the one_page_checkout experiment, and when

Only random.random() is used, with a fixed seed, so everyone gets exactly the same data on any Python 3.
"""

import csv
import json
import random
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

SEED = 2026
START = datetime(2026, 1, 5)                    # a Monday
DAYS = 91                                       # 13 weeks
END = START + timedelta(days=DAYS)
EXP_START, EXP_END = datetime(2026, 3, 2), datetime(2026, 3, 30)    # the one_page_checkout experiment
BUG_START, BUG_END = datetime(2026, 2, 9), datetime(2026, 2, 23)    # an Android payment bug
ONBOARDING_FIX = datetime(2026, 2, 23)          # a new onboarding flow for everyone who signs up from here
OUT = Path(__file__).with_name("pa_data")
CATEGORIES = ["produce", "dairy", "bakery", "pantry", "drinks", "household", "frozen", "snacks"]
CITIES = [("Nairobi", 35), ("Lagos", 30), ("Accra", 20), ("Kigali", 15)]
HOURS = [(7, 3), (8, 5), (9, 5), (10, 4), (11, 4), (12, 6), (13, 5), (14, 3), (15, 3), (16, 4),
         (17, 7), (18, 9), (19, 9), (20, 7), (21, 5), (22, 3)]

R = random.Random(SEED)


def u():
    return R.random()


def pick(options):
    """One value from [(value, weight), ...]."""
    x = u() * sum(w for _, w in options)
    for value, w in options:
        x -= w
        if x < 0:
            return value
    return options[-1][0]


def randint(a, b):
    return a + int(u() * (b - a + 1))


def secs(a, b):
    return timedelta(seconds=randint(a, b))


def start_time(day):
    return START + timedelta(days=day, hours=pick(HOURS), minutes=randint(0, 59), seconds=randint(0, 59))


def gap(t):
    """The time to the next event: usually seconds, sometimes a pause, now and then a long break."""
    x = u()
    if x < 0.025:
        return t + secs(32 * 60, 55 * 60)
    if x < 0.065:
        return t + secs(12 * 60, 25 * 60)
    return t + secs(8, 90)


events = []          # (time, anonymous_id, user_id, event_name, platform, properties)
assignments = {}     # user_id -> (variant, assigned_at)
exposed = set()
orders = [0]


def emit(t, anon, user, name, platform, props=None):
    if t < END:
        events.append((t, anon, user, name, platform, props or {}))


def browse(t, anon, platform, channel):
    """An anonymous visit: maybe a campaign click, then a look around."""
    if channel:
        emit(t, anon, "", "campaign_click", platform, {"channel": channel, "campaign": f"{channel}_q1"})
        t = gap(t)
    if u() < 0.6:
        emit(t, anon, "", "app_open", platform)
        t = gap(t)
    for _ in range(randint(1, 5)):
        item = randint(1, 400)
        emit(t, anon, "", "view_item", platform, {"item_id": item, "category": CATEGORIES[item % 8]})
        t = gap(t)
    return t


def shop(t, anon, user, platform, keen, opened=False):
    """A visit by a signed-up user: browse, and perhaps check out and buy."""
    if EXP_START <= t < EXP_END and user not in assignments:
        assignments[user] = ("treatment" if u() < 0.5 else "control", t)
    if not opened and u() < 0.08:                  # opened the app and left
        emit(t, anon, user, "app_open", platform)
        return t
    if not opened and u() < 0.6:
        emit(t, anon, user, "app_open", platform)
        t = gap(t)
    if u() < 0.4:
        emit(t, anon, user, "search", platform, {"query_length": randint(3, 18)})
        t = gap(t)
    cart = 0
    for _ in range(randint(1, 6)):
        item = randint(1, 400)
        emit(t, anon, user, "view_item", platform, {"item_id": item, "category": CATEGORIES[item % 8]})
        t = gap(t)
        if u() < keen:
            emit(t, anon, user, "add_to_cart", platform, {"item_id": item})
            cart += 1
            t = gap(t)
    if cart and u() < 0.62:
        p = {"ios": 0.72, "android": 0.72, "web": 0.64}[platform]
        if platform == "android" and BUG_START <= t < BUG_END:
            p = 0.44
        if EXP_START <= t < EXP_END and user in assignments:
            variant = assignments[user][0]
            if user not in exposed:
                exposed.add(user)
                emit(t, anon, user, "experiment_exposure", platform,
                     {"experiment": "one_page_checkout", "variant": variant})
            if variant == "treatment":
                p += 0.07
        emit(t, anon, user, "begin_checkout", platform, {"cart_items": cart})
        t += secs(30, 240)
        if u() < p:
            orders[0] += 1
            cents = 1200 + randint(0, 8300)
            emit(t, anon, user, "purchase", platform,
                 {"order_id": f"o{orders[0]:06d}", "revenue": cents / 100, "items": cart + randint(0, 8)})
    return t


def lifetime(user, anon, platform, signup_at, kind, keen):
    """Every visit a user makes after the day they sign up."""
    decay = 1.0
    first = (signup_at - START).days
    for day in range(first + 1, DAYS):
        decay *= {"core": 0.9, "casual": 0.9, "drifter": 0.7}[kind]
        p = {"core": 0.22 + 0.3 * decay, "casual": 0.035 + 0.3 * decay, "drifter": 0.25 * decay}[kind]
        if (START + timedelta(days=day)).weekday() >= 5:
            p *= 1.25
        if u() < p:
            for _ in range(2 if u() < 0.25 else 1):
                t = start_time(day)
                if u() < 0.08:
                    emit(t, anon, user, "campaign_click", platform, {"channel": "email", "campaign": "weekly_offers"})
                    t = gap(t)
                shop(t, anon, user, platform, keen)


def main():
    users = []
    visitors = 0
    for day in range(DAYS):
        weekend = (START + timedelta(days=day)).weekday() >= 5
        n = int((44 + 0.15 * day) * (1.2 if weekend else 1.0) * (0.85 + 0.3 * u()))
        for _ in range(n):
            visitors += 1
            anon = f"a{visitors:05d}"
            platform = pick([("ios", 38), ("android", 47), ("web", 15)])
            first = pick([(None, 42), ("paid_search", 20), ("paid_social", 20), ("referral", 18)])
            visits = pick([(1, 50), (2, 30), (3, 20)])
            p_signup = {None: 0.46, "paid_search": 0.5, "paid_social": 0.34, "referral": 0.62}[first]
            if platform == "web":
                p_signup *= 0.85
            signs_up = u() < p_signup
            t = start_time(day)
            for v in range(visits):
                channel = first if v == 0 else pick([(None, 55), ("retargeting", 25), ("paid_search", 12),
                                                      ("paid_social", 8)])
                t = browse(t, anon, platform, channel)
                if v < visits - 1:
                    t += timedelta(hours=randint(8, 96), minutes=randint(0, 59))
            if not signs_up or t >= END:
                continue
            user = f"u{len(users) + 1:05d}"
            emit(t, anon, user, "sign_up", platform, {"method": pick([("email", 55), ("google", 30), ("phone", 15)])})
            weights = [("core", 20), ("casual", 35), ("drifter", 45)]
            if first == "paid_social":
                weights = [("core", 12), ("casual", 30), ("drifter", 58)]
            if t >= ONBOARDING_FIX:
                weights = [(k, w + (8 if k == "core" else -8 if k == "drifter" else 0)) for k, w in weights]
            kind = pick(weights)
            keen = {"core": 0.5, "casual": 0.4, "drifter": 0.3}[kind]
            if u() < 0.5:
                shop(gap(t), anon, user, platform, keen, opened=True)
            users.append((user, t, platform, pick(CITIES), False))
            lifetime(user, anon, platform, t, kind, keen)

    for i, platform in enumerate(["ios", "android", "web"], 1):     # the QA team's test accounts
        user, anon = f"qa{i:02d}", f"qa-device-{i}"
        users.append((user, START, platform, "Nairobi", True))
        for day in range(DAYS):
            if (START + timedelta(days=day)).weekday() < 5:
                for _ in range(2):
                    shop(start_time(day), anon, user, platform, 0.9)

    events.sort(key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1], e[3]))
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    rows = 0
    with open(OUT / "raw_events.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["event_id", "anonymous_id", "user_id", "event_time", "event_name", "platform", "properties"])
        for n, (t, anon, user, name, platform, props) in enumerate(events, 1):
            row = [f"e{n:07d}", anon, user, t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), name, platform,
                   json.dumps(props, separators=(",", ":"))]
            for _ in range(2 if u() < 0.004 else 1):         # a retried upload sends the same event twice
                w.writerow(row)
                rows += 1
    with open(OUT / "users.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["user_id", "signup_time", "platform", "city", "is_internal"])
        for user, t, platform, city, internal in sorted(users):
            w.writerow([user, t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), platform, city, str(internal).lower()])
    with open(OUT / "assignments.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["user_id", "experiment", "variant", "assigned_at"])
        for user, (variant, t) in sorted(assignments.items()):
            w.writerow([user, "one_page_checkout", variant, t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")])
    print(f"Wrote {rows} raw events from {visitors} visitors, {len(users)} accounts and "
          f"{len(assignments)} experiment assignments to {OUT.name}/")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Helpers for every lab: open Basketful's data in DuckDB, and print a query's result as a plain table.

    from pa_common import connect, show
    con = connect()                      # views: raw_events, users, assignments, and events if clean_events.sql exists
    show(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM events")
"""

from pathlib import Path

import duckdb

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
DATA = HERE / "pa_data"
RAW = {"event_id": "VARCHAR", "anonymous_id": "VARCHAR", "user_id": "VARCHAR", "event_time": "TIMESTAMP",
       "event_name": "VARCHAR", "platform": "VARCHAR", "properties": "VARCHAR"}
USERS = {"user_id": "VARCHAR", "signup_time": "TIMESTAMP", "platform": "VARCHAR", "city": "VARCHAR",
         "is_internal": "BOOLEAN"}
ASSIGNMENTS = {"user_id": "VARCHAR", "experiment": "VARCHAR", "variant": "VARCHAR", "assigned_at": "TIMESTAMP"}


def connect():
    """An in-memory DuckDB database with a view over each CSV file, plus the clean events view
    defined in clean_events.sql (lab 1) once that file exists."""
    if not (DATA / "raw_events.csv").exists():
        raise SystemExit("No data yet: run python make_events.py first.")
    con = duckdb.connect()
    for name, columns in [("raw_events", RAW), ("users", USERS), ("assignments", ASSIGNMENTS)]:
        path = (DATA / f"{name}.csv").as_posix()
        con.execute(f"CREATE VIEW {name} AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('{path}', header = true, columns = {columns})")
    clean = HERE / "clean_events.sql"
    if clean.exists():
        con.execute(clean.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    return con


def _cell(v):
    return "NULL" if v is None else str(v)


def show(con, sql, title=None):
    """Run a query and print its result as an aligned table, numbers on the right."""
    rel = con.sql(sql)
    columns, rows = rel.columns, [[_cell(v) for v in r] for r in rel.fetchall()]
    numeric = [all(r[i].replace(".", "", 1).replace("-", "", 1).isdigit() for r in rows if r[i] != "NULL")
               for i in range(len(columns))]
    widths = [max([len(c)] + [len(r[i]) for r in rows]) for i, c in enumerate(columns)]
    if title:
        print(f"\n{title}")
    print("  ".join(c.rjust(w) if n else c.ljust(w) for c, w, n in zip(columns, widths, numeric)))
    for r in rows:
        print("  ".join(v.rjust(w) if n else v.ljust(w) for v, w, n in zip(r, widths, numeric)))
    print(f"({len(rows)} row{'s' if len(rows) != 1 else ''})")

-- The clean events view every later query starts from: one row per event, QA accounts left out,
-- and anonymous events from before sign-up linked to the user who signed up on that device.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW events AS
WITH deduplicated AS (
    -- TODO 1: keep one row per event_id (retried uploads sent some events twice)
    SELECT *
    FROM raw_events
),
identities AS (
    -- TODO 2: one row per anonymous_id that has ever signed in, with its user_id
    SELECT CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS anonymous_id, CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS user_id
)
SELECT d.event_id,
       d.anonymous_id,
       COALESCE(d.user_id, i.user_id) AS user_id,
       d.event_time,
       d.event_name,
       d.platform,
       d.properties ->> '$.channel' AS channel,
       CAST(d.properties ->> '$.revenue' AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS revenue,
       d.properties
FROM deduplicated AS d
LEFT JOIN identities AS i USING (anonymous_id)
LEFT JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = COALESCE(d.user_id, i.user_id)
-- TODO 3: leave out the QA team's accounts (users.is_internal), but keep visitors who never signed up
WHERE true;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW active_days AS
-- TODO 1: one row per user and day on which they did something meaningful (search, view_item,

SELECT CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS user_id, CAST(NULL AS DATE) AS day
"""

SNAPSHOT = """

modules.title: Sessions and funnels
modules.summary: Use window functions to turn an event stream into sessions and ordered funnels, then read a funnel by platform and week to find where, and when, users drop off.

lessons.title: Window functions for event streams
objectives: Use LAG and LEAD to compare each event with its neighbours
Choose a window frame, ROWS or RANGE, for rolling metrics
Make window results repeatable with a deterministic order
key_points: Event analysis is mostly about sequences, so it leans on window functions partitioned by user or device and ordered by time: LAG(event_time) returns the previous event's time and LEAD(event_time) the next one's.

Ties in a window's ORDER BY make results depend on how the engine happens to read the rows; add a unique tie-breaker, as in ORDER BY event_time, event_id, so that every run numbers the events the same way.

A frame limits the rows a window aggregate sees: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW takes the six rows before, while RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAYS PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW takes rows whose date is within six days, so missing days don't stretch the window.
A running SUM over a 0/1 flag numbers runs of consecutive rows: each row where the flag is 1 starts a new run, which is the basis of sessionisation and of finding streaks.
MIN(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id), or FIRST_VALUE, attaches each user's first event time to every one of their rows without a self-join, ready for measuring time since first use.

lessons.title: Sessionisation
objectives: Split each device's events into sessions with an inactivity gap
Measure sessions: how many, how long and how many events
Explain how the gap chosen changes the results
key_points: A session is a burst of activity from one device or user; the usual rule starts a new session when the time since the previous event is longer than an inactivity timeout, often 30 minutes.

In SQL, LAG gives each event's previous time, a CASE sets a flag to 1 when there's no previous event or the gap exceeds the timeout, and a running SUM of the flag numbers the sessions, making a session_id such as anonymous_id || '-' || n.

The timeout is a choice, not a fact: a shorter one splits pauses into extra sessions and a longer one merges separate visits, so state the timeout with any session metric and check how sensitive the counts are to it.

A session's length is its last event's time minus its first, so a one-event session lasts zero seconds; report the median length and the share of single-event sessions, not a mean pulled up by a long tail.

Sessionise by device to include visits before sign-up, or by user to join one person's devices; client-generated session ids follow each SDK's own rules, so deriving sessions from timestamps gives one definition on every platform.

lessons.title: Ordered funnels and conversion windows
objectives: Build an ordered funnel at session or user level
Apply a conversion window to a user funnel
Compute step and overall conversion rates
key_points: A funnel counts the units that reach each step of a path, such as view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout and purchase; a step only counts if it happens after the step before, which is what makes the funnel ordered.

The unit matters: a session funnel asks whether one visit went all the way, while a user funnel asks whether a person got there within a conversion window, such as purchasing within 7 days of their first add to cart.

A compact build pivots each unit's first time at each step with MIN(event_time) FILTER (WHERE event_name = ...), then counts units whose step times are in order; when steps repeat, a strict funnel instead joins each step to the first later occurrence of the next.

Step conversion divides each step by the one before and overall conversion divides the last step by the first; report both, and the number of users lost at each step, since the biggest absolute loss is where a fix reaches the most people.
Session funnels undercount when a long pause splits one shopping trip in two: the cart in one session and the purchase in the next look like an abandoned cart and a purchase from nowhere.

lessons.title: Reading a funnel: segments, trends and time to convert
objectives: Segment a funnel by platform and week to locate a problem
Measure time to convert with medians
Avoid the common misreadings of funnel changes
key_points: Break a funnel down by the dimensions a fix would target, such as platform, app version, country and week: a drop confined to one platform for two weeks points to a release or an outage, not to customers changing their minds.
Check each segment's size before reading its rate: a step rate from 60 checkouts moves by several points from chance alone, while one from 600 is far steadier.

An overall rate can change because the mix of segments changed, such as more traffic from a low-converting channel, while no segment changed at all (Simpson's paradox), so compare rates within segments.
Time to convert is skewed by a few slow users, so report the median and a high percentile, such as MEDIAN() or quantile_cont(x, 0.9) of the minutes from first view to purchase, rather than the mean.
A funnel shows where users drop off, not why: pair it with release notes, error logs, support tickets or user research, and test a fix with an experiment before claiming it worked.

-- The clean events view every later query starts from: one row per event, QA accounts left out,
-- and anonymous events from before sign-up linked to the user who signed up on that device.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW events AS
WITH deduplicated AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM raw_events
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY event_time) = 1
),
identities AS (
    SELECT anonymous_id, MIN(user_id) AS user_id
    FROM deduplicated
    WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY anonymous_id
)
SELECT d.event_id,
       d.anonymous_id,
       COALESCE(d.user_id, i.user_id) AS user_id,
       d.event_time,
       d.event_name,
       d.platform,
       d.properties ->> '$.channel' AS channel,
       CAST(d.properties ->> '$.revenue' AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS revenue,
       d.properties
FROM deduplicated AS d
LEFT JOIN identities AS i USING (anonymous_id)
LEFT JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = COALESCE(d.user_id, i.user_id)
WHERE NOT COALESCE(u.is_internal, false);

"""Lab 2: split each device's events into sessions, then build the checkout funnel and find where it broke."""

from pa_common import connect, show

SESSIONS = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sessionised AS
WITH ordered AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY anonymous_id ORDER BY event_time, event_id) AS previous_time
    FROM events
),
flagged AS (
    -- TODO 1: new_session = 1 for a device's first event, or after a gap of more than 30 minutes; else 0
    SELECT *, 1 AS new_session
    FROM ordered
)
-- TODO 2: number each device's sessions with a running SUM of new_session (ordered by event_time, event_id)
-- and build session_id from anonymous_id, '-' and that number
SELECT *, event_id AS session_id
FROM flagged
"""

SUMMARY = """
WITH per_session AS (
    SELECT session_id, COUNT(*) AS events,
           date_diff('second', MIN(event_time), MAX(event_time)) / 60 AS minutes
    FROM sessionised
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sessions,
       ROUND(AVG(events), 2) AS events_per_session,
       ROUND(MEDIAN(minutes), 1) AS median_minutes,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE events = 1) AS single_event_sessions
FROM per_session
"""

THRESHOLDS = """
SELECT gap_minutes,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE previous_time IS NULL
                          OR event_time - previous_time > gap_minutes * INTERVAL 1 MINUTE) AS sessions
FROM (SELECT * FROM sessionised), (VALUES (10), (30), (60)) AS g(gap_minutes)
GROUP BY gap_minutes
ORDER BY gap_minutes
"""

FUNNEL = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW session_steps AS
SELECT session_id,
       ANY_VALUE(platform) AS platform,
       MIN(event_time) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'view_item') AS viewed,
       MIN(event_time) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart') AS added,
       MIN(event_time) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'begin_checkout') AS checked_out,

FROM sessionised
GROUP BY session_id

FROM session_steps
WHERE purchased >= viewed

modules.title: Cohorts and retention
modules.summary: Group users by when they started, build retention tables and curves that handle cohorts still in progress, and account for growth: new, retained, resurrected and churned users.

lessons.title: Cohorts: comparing users who started together
objectives: Explain why cohorts beat aggregate metrics for judging retention
Build acquisition and behavioural cohorts
Read a cohort table down its columns and along its rows
key_points: A cohort is a group of users who share a starting point, usually the week or month they signed up; comparing cohorts shows how the product treats new users now compared with earlier ones.

Aggregate metrics mix cohorts of different ages: in a fast-growing product, overall retention can fall while every cohort retains better, because young cohorts, which haven't settled yet, make up more of the total.

Acquisition cohorts group users by start date; behavioural cohorts group them by something they did, such as buying in their first week, which shows association with retention, not that the behaviour causes it.
A cohort table has one row per cohort and one column per period since the start: reading down a column compares cohorts at the same age, and reading along a row follows one cohort as it ages.
Count periods from each user's own sign-up, (activity_day - signup_day) // 7 for weeks, rather than calendar weeks, so that week 1 means the same span of time for everyone.

lessons.title: Retention curves and cohorts still in progress
objectives: Compute N-week, unbounded and bracket retention
Handle cohorts whose periods haven't finished
Read the shape of a retention curve
key_points: N-week retention is the share of a cohort active in week N; unbounded retention counts users active in week N or any later week, so it can only fall as N grows and is never lower than N-week retention for the same N.
Bracket retention uses wider periods, such as days 1-7 and 8-14, which suits products people use weekly, like a grocery shop, better than day-by-day retention does.
Count a cohort in week N only once week N has ended for all of its users; a cohort whose week 4 is still under way shows falsely low retention, so leave those cells empty (NULL), never zero.
To draw one curve, pool every user whose week N has finished and divide the active ones by them; the denominator shrinks as N grows, so the late points rest on fewer, older users and are noisier.
A curve that flattens means a core of users keeps coming back; one that keeps sliding towards zero means the product eventually loses almost everyone, however good the first weeks look.

A before-and-after comparison of cohorts, such as retention before and after a new onboarding flow, can also reflect seasonality or a change in channel mix; confirm it with an experiment or by comparing within channels.

lessons.title: Churn, resurrection and growth accounting
objectives: Split active users into new, retained and resurrected, and count churn
Build growth accounting in SQL with LAG and LEAD
Use the quick ratio, and know its limits
key_points: Growth accounting splits each period's active users into new (their first active period), retained (also active the period before) and resurrected (back after a gap), and counts churned users: active last period but not this one.
The parts must add up: this period's active users = new + retained + resurrected, and last period's active users = retained + churned; run that check on every growth accounting query.

In SQL, reduce activity to one row per user per week; LAG and LEAD over each user's weeks give the previous and next active weeks, so a previous week exactly 7 days earlier means retained and an earlier one means resurrected.
The quick ratio, (new + resurrected) / churned, compares users gained with users lost: above 1 the active base is growing, but a high ratio driven by heavy acquisition can still hide poor retention.
Choose the period from how often the product is naturally used: a week without activity may mean churn for a messaging app, but only a normal gap for a weekly grocery shop or a monthly bill payment.

"""Lab 3: weekly retention by sign-up cohort, the retention curve, and growth accounting."""

from pa_common import connect, show

ACTIVITY = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW active_days AS
SELECT DISTINCT e.user_id, CAST(e.event_time AS DATE) AS day
FROM events AS e
JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = e.user_id AND e.event_time >= u.signup_time
WHERE e.event_name IN ('search', 'view_item', 'add_to_cart', 'begin_checkout', 'purchase');

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW user_weeks AS
SELECT a.user_id,
       CAST(u.signup_time AS DATE) AS signup_day,
       CAST(date_trunc('week', u.signup_time) AS DATE) AS cohort_week,
       (a.day - CAST(u.signup_time AS DATE)) // 7 AS week_n
FROM active_days AS a
JOIN users AS u USING (user_id);
"""

COHORT_TABLE = """
-- TODO 1: one row per cohort_week with its number of (non-QA) users, then w1, w2, w4 and w8: the share
-- of the cohort active in week n after sign-up (from user_weeks), to 3 places. Leave a cell NULL until
-- week n has ended for the cohort's last sign-up day: cohort_week + 7 * n + 12 <= DATE '2026-04-05'
SELECT 'TODO' AS todo
"""

CURVE = """
WITH weeks AS (SELECT CAST(range AS INTEGER) AS week_n FROM range(1, 11)),
eligible AS (
    SELECT w.week_n, u.user_id
    FROM weeks AS w
    JOIN users AS u ON NOT u.is_internal
                   AND CAST(u.signup_time AS DATE) + 7 * w.week_n + 6 <= DATE '2026-04-05'
)
SELECT e.week_n,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id) AS eligible_users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT uw.user_id) AS active_users,
       ROUND(active_users / eligible_users, 3) AS retention
FROM eligible AS e
LEFT JOIN user_weeks AS uw ON uw.user_id = e.user_id AND uw.week_n = e.week_n
GROUP BY e.week_n
ORDER BY e.week_n
"""

ONBOARDING = """
SELECT CASE WHEN u.signup_time >= TIMESTAMP '2026-02-23' THEN 'from 23 Feb' ELSE 'before 23 Feb' END AS signed_up,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS eligible_users,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT uw.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 3) AS week2_retention
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN user_weeks AS uw ON uw.user_id = u.user_id AND uw.week_n = 2
WHERE NOT u.is_internal
  AND CAST(u.signup_time AS DATE) + 20 <= DATE '2026-04-05'
GROUP BY signed_up
ORDER BY signed_up
"""

GROWTH = """
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id, CAST(date_trunc('week', day) AS DATE) AS week
    FROM active_days
),
flagged AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(week) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY week) AS previous_week,
           LEAD(week) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY week) AS next_week
    FROM weekly
),
states AS (
    -- TODO 2: per week, active users, then new_users (no earlier active week), retained (the previous
    -- active week is exactly 7 days earlier) and resurrected (the previous active week is earlier still)
    SELECT week, COUNT(*) AS active, 0 AS new_users, 0 AS retained, 0 AS resurrected
    FROM flagged
    GROUP BY week
),
churn AS (
    -- TODO 3: per week, the users who were active the week before but not this week
    SELECT week + 7 AS week, 1 AS churned
    FROM flagged
    GROUP BY week + 7
)
SELECT s.week, s.active, s.new_users, s.retained, s.resurrected, c.churned,
       ROUND((s.new_users + s.resurrected) / c.churned, 2) AS quick_ratio
FROM states AS s
JOIN churn AS c USING (week)
WHERE s.week BETWEEN DATE '2026-02-02' AND DATE '2026-03-30'
ORDER BY s.week
"""

con = connect()
con.execute(ACTIVITY)
show(con, COHORT_TABLE, "Share of each weekly cohort active in week n after sign-up (blank until it's complete)")
show(con, CURVE, "The retention curve: every user whose week n has finished")
show(con, ONBOARDING, "Week-2 retention before and after the new onboarding flow")
show(con, GROWTH, "Growth accounting by week")

hints: A cohort's last sign-up day is cohort_week + 6, and its week n ends 7 * n + 6 days after that: cohort_week + 7 * n + 12.
LEAD(week) is NULL for a user's last active week, and that user churned the week after, unless it's the data's last week.
Use range() for a series of whole numbers, and cast it to INTEGER before adding it to a DATE.

modules.title: Attribution: giving conversions their credit
modules.summary: Match conversions to the marketing touches before them, share the credit with single-touch and multi-touch rules in SQL, and see why attribution isn't the same as incrementality.

lessons.title: Touchpoints, lookback windows and single-touch rules
objectives: Match conversions to the touches before them within a lookback window
Compare first-touch and last-touch attribution
Report conversions with no tracked touch honestly
key_points: Attribution shares the credit for a conversion, such as a sign-up or a first purchase, among the marketing touches before it: campaign clicks, ad visits and referral links, each recorded with its channel.

Only touches before the conversion and inside a lookback window count, such as the 14 days before sign-up; leave out the time condition and the query credits touches that came afterwards, like offers emailed to existing customers.

First-touch gives all the credit to the touch that started the journey, which favours channels that bring new people in; last-touch gives it to the final touch, which favours channels that close, such as retargeting ads.

Conversions with no tracked touch are direct or organic visits, or journeys whose touches were lost to blocked cookies, consent choices or app-store redirects; report their share rather than spreading them over the channels.
Touches usually happen before sign-up, on an anonymous device id, so stitch identities first; without it, most sign-ups appear to have no touch at all.

lessons.title: Multi-touch rules, and what attribution can't tell you
objectives: Compute linear and position-based credit with window functions
Check that an attribution query conserves conversions
Distinguish attribution from incrementality
key_points: Linear attribution splits a conversion equally across its n touches, 1/n each; position-based (U-shaped) gives 40% each to the first and last touch and shares the other 20% among the touches between, with special cases for one or two touches.

In SQL, number each conversion's touches with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY the conversion ORDER BY time, id) and count them with COUNT(*) OVER (the same partition), then work out each touch's credit with CASE.
Whatever the rule, each conversion's credits must add up to 1, so every model's channel totals add up to the same number of attributed conversions; check this before comparing models.

Time-decay rules give more credit to touches closer to the conversion, for example halving a touch's weight for every 7 days before it; data-driven models instead learn weights from paths that did and didn't convert.

Rule-based attribution redistributes the same conversions by convention, so changing the rule moves budget without measuring what any channel caused; incrementality, the conversions that wouldn't have happened otherwise, needs an experiment such as a holdout group or a geographic test.

"""Lab 4: give each sign-up's credit to the campaign clicks before it, under four attribution rules."""

from pa_common import connect, show

TOUCHES = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW signup_touches AS
WITH signups AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time AS signed_up_at
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'sign_up'
)
SELECT s.user_id, e.channel, e.event_time,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY s.user_id ORDER BY e.event_time, e.event_id) AS touch_n,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY s.user_id) AS touches
FROM signups AS s
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.user_id = s.user_id
 AND e.event_name = 'campaign_click'
 -- TODO 1: only clicks at or before the sign-up, and no more than 14 days before it
"""

COVERAGE = """
SELECT COUNT(*) AS signups,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM signup_touches)) AS with_a_touch,
       ROUND(1 - with_a_touch / signups, 3) AS share_without_a_touch,
       (SELECT ROUND(AVG(touches), 2) FROM signup_touches WHERE touch_n = 1) AS touches_per_touched_signup
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'sign_up'
"""

CREDIT = """
WITH credit AS (
    SELECT channel,
           -- TODO 2: each touch's credit under each rule; every sign-up's credits must add up to 1.
           -- position_based: 40% each to the first and last touch and 20% shared by the ones between
           -- (one touch gets 1.0, and each of two touches 0.5)
           0.0 AS first_touch,
           0.0 AS last_touch,
           0.0 AS linear,
           0.0 AS position_based
    FROM signup_touches
)
SELECT channel,
       ROUND(SUM(first_touch), 1) AS first_touch,
       ROUND(SUM(last_touch), 1) AS last_touch,
       ROUND(SUM(linear), 1) AS linear,
       ROUND(SUM(position_based), 1) AS position_based
FROM credit
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY first_touch DESC
"""

TRAP = """
SELECT e.channel, COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id) AS signups_credited_wrongly
FROM events AS s
JOIN events AS e ON e.user_id = s.user_id AND e.event_name = 'campaign_click' AND e.event_time > s.event_time
WHERE s.event_name = 'sign_up'
GROUP BY e.channel
ORDER BY e.channel
"""

con = connect()
con.execute(TOUCHES)
show(con, COVERAGE, "Sign-ups with a campaign click in the 14 days before")
show(con, CREDIT, "Sign-ups credited to each channel, by rule")
show(con, TRAP, "Clicks after sign-up: the ones a missing time condition would credit")

hints: touch_n = touches picks the last touch, because touches is the count over the same partition.
For four touches, position-based credit is 0.4, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.4: the 0.2 is shared by the two in the middle.
Sum the credits per user and check every user's total is 1: SELECT user_id, SUM(linear) FROM credit GROUP BY user_id HAVING ABS(SUM(linear) - 1) > 1e-9 should return nothing.

modules.title: Experiment readouts from event data
modules.summary: Build an A/B test readout in SQL: join assignments to events, choose the population and windows, check the split, compute differences and intervals for conversion, means and ratios, and decide.

lessons.title: Assignment, exposure and the analysis population
objectives: Join an assignment log to outcome events correctly
Choose between all-assigned and triggered analysis
Check the sample ratio and the logging before reading results
key_points: An experiment's data has two parts: the assignment log, saying which variant each user got and when, and the events that measure outcomes; join them on the unit that was randomised, usually the user.

Exposure is the moment a user could first notice the change, such as reaching checkout; analysing only exposed users (a triggered analysis) is valid when exposure happens the same way in both variants, which holds when the change can't act before it.

Including users who were never exposed dilutes the effect: they add the same behaviour to both groups, so the difference in rates shrinks while the noise doesn't, and a real effect becomes harder to detect.

Measure outcomes from each user's first exposure inside a fixed window, such as 24 hours or 7 days, and only for users whose whole window ended before the test did, so every user is measured for the same length of time.

Check the split first: a sample ratio mismatch, such as 52/48 in a 50/50 test, shows in a chi-square statistic on the counts; with two groups, above 3.84 is significant at the 5% level, and many teams act only above 10.83 (p < 0.001).
Remove internal and test accounts from both the assignment log and the outcomes, and check that the variant recorded in exposure events matches the assignment log.

lessons.title: Computing the readout in SQL
objectives: Reduce experiment data to one row per user
Compute differences and 95% intervals for proportions and means
Treat ratio metrics such as average order value correctly
key_points: First reduce the data to one row per user with their variant and outcomes, such as converted (0 or 1), revenue and orders; then every mean and variance comes from rows of the unit that was randomised.
For conversion rates the standard error of the difference is SQRT(p_c(1 - p_c)/n_c + p_t(1 - p_t)/n_t), and the 95% interval is the difference plus or minus 1.96 standard errors.

For a mean such as revenue per user, use each group's VAR_SAMP: the standard error is SQRT(var_c/n_c + var_t/n_t); revenue is skewed, so with small groups or extreme outliers check the interval with a bootstrap over users.

A ratio metric such as average order value (revenue / orders) is measured per order, not per randomised user; compute it as a ratio of per-user sums and get its standard error from the delta method or a bootstrap over users, never by treating orders as independent.

Report each metric's absolute difference, relative lift (difference / control) and interval: one primary metric chosen in advance, secondary metrics that explain it, and guardrail metrics that mustn't get worse.

lessons.title: Writing the readout and making the decision
objectives: Structure an experiment readout
Interpret intervals, guardrails and segments without over-claiming
Recommend ship, don't ship, iterate or extend
key_points: A readout states the hypothesis, the population and dates, the checks made (sample ratio, exposure logging, data quality), the primary result with its interval, the secondary and guardrail results, and the decision with its reasons.

An interval that excludes zero says the effect is unlikely to be zero, and its width says how precisely it's known: a lift between 1 and 12 points is probably real but could be small, so plan with the cautious end.

A guardrail that moves the wrong way without a significant result, such as a lower average order value, is a reason to keep watching it after launch or to test longer, not something to leave out of the readout.
Segments cut after the fact, by platform or city for instance, are exploratory: among many cuts some differ by chance, so treat a striking segment as a hypothesis for the next test.

Decide among ship, don't ship, iterate and extend by weighing the evidence against the cost of being wrong, and write down what would change the decision, such as the guardrail's trend over the first month.

"""Lab 5: read out the one_page_checkout experiment from the assignment table and the events."""

from pa_common import connect, show

SRM = """
WITH assigned AS (
    SELECT a.variant, COUNT(*) AS users
    FROM assignments AS a
    JOIN users AS u USING (user_id)
    WHERE a.experiment = 'one_page_checkout' AND NOT u.is_internal
    GROUP BY a.variant
),
totals AS (SELECT SUM(users) AS total FROM assigned),
-- TODO 1: the chi-square statistic: the sum over both variants of (users - expected) ^ 2 / expected,
-- where expected = total / 2
srm AS (SELECT 0 AS chi_square)
SELECT a.variant, a.users,
       ROUND(a.users / t.total, 4) AS share,
       ROUND(srm.chi_square, 3) AS chi_square
FROM assigned AS a, totals AS t, srm
ORDER BY a.variant
"""

EXPOSED = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW exposed AS
SELECT e.user_id, a.variant, MIN(e.event_time) AS exposed_at
FROM events AS e
JOIN assignments AS a ON a.user_id = e.user_id AND a.experiment = 'one_page_checkout'
WHERE e.event_name = 'experiment_exposure'
GROUP BY e.user_id, a.variant
"""

OUTCOMES = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW outcomes AS
SELECT x.user_id, x.variant,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(p.event_id) > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.revenue), 0) AS revenue,
       COUNT(p.event_id) AS orders
FROM exposed AS x
LEFT JOIN events AS p
  ON p.user_id = x.user_id
 AND p.event_name = 'purchase'
 -- TODO 2: only purchases in the 24 hours from the user's first exposure
-- TODO 3: only users first exposed before 29 March, so every user's 24 hours end inside the test
GROUP BY x.user_id, x.variant
"""

READOUT = """
WITH v AS (
    SELECT variant, COUNT(*) AS n,
           AVG(converted) AS conversion,
           AVG(revenue) AS revenue_per_user,
           VAR_SAMP(revenue) AS revenue_variance,
           SUM(revenue) / SUM(orders) AS aov,
           AVG(orders) AS orders_per_user,
           VAR_SAMP(orders) AS orders_variance,
           COVAR_SAMP(revenue, orders) AS covariance
    FROM outcomes
    GROUP BY variant
),
s AS (
    SELECT *,
           0 AS conversion_se2,  -- TODO 4: a proportion's squared standard error, p(1 - p) / n
           revenue_variance / n AS revenue_se2,
           (revenue_variance - 2 * aov * covariance + aov ^ 2 * orders_variance)
               / (n * orders_per_user ^ 2) AS aov_se2
    FROM v
),
c AS (SELECT * FROM s WHERE variant = 'control'),
t AS (SELECT * FROM s WHERE variant = 'treatment')
SELECT 'conversion' AS metric, c.n AS n_control, t.n AS n_treatment,
       ROUND(c.conversion, 4) AS control, ROUND(t.conversion, 4) AS treatment,
       ROUND(t.conversion - c.conversion, 4) AS difference,
       ROUND(t.conversion - c.conversion - 1.96 * SQRT(c.conversion_se2 + t.conversion_se2), 4) AS ci_low,
       ROUND(t.conversion - c.conversion + 1.96 * SQRT(c.conversion_se2 + t.conversion_se2), 4) AS ci_high
FROM c, t
UNION ALL
SELECT 'revenue_per_user', c.n, t.n,
       ROUND(c.revenue_per_user, 2), ROUND(t.revenue_per_user, 2),
       ROUND(t.revenue_per_user - c.revenue_per_user, 2),
       ROUND(t.revenue_per_user - c.revenue_per_user - 1.96 * SQRT(c.revenue_se2 + t.revenue_se2), 2),
       ROUND(t.revenue_per_user - c.revenue_per_user + 1.96 * SQRT(c.revenue_se2 + t.revenue_se2), 2)
FROM c, t
UNION ALL
SELECT 'average_order_value', c.n, t.n,
       ROUND(c.aov, 2), ROUND(t.aov, 2), ROUND(t.aov - c.aov, 2),
       ROUND(t.aov - c.aov - 1.96 * SQRT(c.aov_se2 + t.aov_se2), 2),
       ROUND(t.aov - c.aov + 1.96 * SQRT(c.aov_se2 + t.aov_se2), 2)
FROM c, t
"""

DILUTED = """
WITH population AS (
    SELECT a.user_id, a.variant,
           a.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM exposed) AS was_exposed,
           EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM events AS p
                   WHERE p.user_id = a.user_id AND p.event_name = 'purchase'
                     AND p.event_time >= a.assigned_at AND p.event_time < TIMESTAMP '2026-03-30') AS bought
    FROM assignments AS a
    JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = a.user_id AND NOT u.is_internal
)
SELECT 'all assigned' AS analysed, variant, COUNT(*) AS users,
       SUM(CAST(bought AS INTEGER)) AS buyers, ROUND(AVG(CAST(bought AS INTEGER)), 4) AS conversion
FROM population GROUP BY variant
UNION ALL
SELECT 'exposed only', variant, COUNT(*), SUM(CAST(bought AS INTEGER)), ROUND(AVG(CAST(bought AS INTEGER)), 4)
FROM population WHERE was_exposed GROUP BY variant
ORDER BY analysed, variant
"""

con = connect()
show(con, SRM, "Assignments by variant, without QA accounts, and the sample ratio check")
con.execute(EXPOSED)
con.execute(OUTCOMES)
show(con, "SELECT variant, COUNT(*) AS exposed_users FROM exposed GROUP BY variant ORDER BY variant",
     "Users who reached checkout during the test")
show(con, READOUT, "Readout: the 24 hours after first exposure, for users exposed 2-28 March (95% intervals)")
show(con, DILUTED, "Bought during the test: every assigned user, then only those exposed")

hints: ^ is the power operator in DuckDB, so (users - total / 2) ^ 2 squares the difference.
Purchases need the time conditions in the LEFT JOIN's ON clause: in WHERE they would turn the LEFT JOIN into an inner join and drop users who didn't buy.
Exposures after 28 March would get less than 24 hours of the test's experience, because the test ended on 30 March.

project.title: A quarterly product review for Basketful
project.brief: Basketful's product lead wants this quarter's review built from the event log rather than from screenshots of dashboards. Using the course data (or your own product's events, in the same shape), build a small, reusable metrics layer in DuckDB and answer five questions with it. Is engagement growing (DAU, WAU, MAU and stickiness)? Where does the purchase funnel lose the most people, by platform and week? Did the onboarding flow launched on 23 February improve retention, and how sure can anyone be without an experiment? Which channels bring sign-ups who stay, looking at week-4 retention by first-touch channel, and how much do the attribution rules disagree? And should one_page_checkout ship? Write it up as a memo of at most two pages for the product team, with tables or charts, and say plainly what the data can't tell you.
